lessons.title: DC and AC Wiring Basics for Solar Pumping
lessons.body: Solar pumps can run on DC (direct current) from panels or AC (alternating current) from an inverter. Most small dam pumps use DC because it avoids the cost and losses of an inverter. DC flows one way, from panel to pump. AC changes direction many times per second. In Africa, many pumps are DC for simplicity. You must match voltage: a 24V pump needs a 24V panel array. Panels are wired in series to add voltage, parallel to add current. For a 24V system, two 12V panels in series give 24V. Use MC4 connectors for DC. They are waterproof and color-coded: red for positive, black for negative. Never mix them. DC arcs are harder to break than AC, so use DC-rated switches and breakers. For AC, you need an inverter. Inverters come in 12V, 24V, 48V DC input and 220V AC output. Use 3-core cable for AC: live (brown), neutral (blue), earth (green/yellow). AC wiring must be in conduit to protect from sun and rain. In Africa, voltage drop over long distances is a big problem. Keep DC cable runs short. For a 500W pump at 24V, current is about 21A. That needs at least 6mmÂ² copper cable for runs up to 20m. For AC, 220V at 500W is only 2.3A, so 1.5mmÂ² is enough. But AC inverters are expensive and less efficient. Most dam sites use DC direct. Always use fuses on positive line. A 25A fuse for that 21A pump. Use a disconnect switch near the pump for maintenance. Label all wires. In Africa, dust and heat degrade insulation. Use UV-resistant cable. Check connections monthly. Tighten terminals because heat expands and contracts them. Never work on live wires. Turn off panels first.

lessons.title: Cable Sizing and Voltage Drop Calculations
lessons.body: Voltage drop is the loss of voltage as current flows through cable. Too much drop and your pump won't start or will run slow. In solar pumping, keep drop under 3% for best performance. The formula: Voltage Drop = (2 x Length x Current x Resistance) / 1000. Length is one-way in meters. Resistance for copper: 1.5mmÂ² = 12.1 ohms per 1000m, 2.5mmÂ² = 7.4, 4mmÂ² = 4.6, 6mmÂ² = 3.1, 10mmÂ² = 1.8. For a 24V system, 3% of 24V is 0.72V. Say you have a 300W pump, so current = 300/24 = 12.5A. If cable run is 30m one-way, using 4mmÂ²: drop = (2 x 30 x 12.5 x 4.6)/1000 = 3.45V. That's 14% â too high. You need 10mmÂ²: drop = (2 x 30 x 12.5 x 1.8)/1000 = 1.35V, still 5.6%. For 30m, you might need 16mmÂ². Better to move panels closer. In Africa, cable is expensive. So design pump close to dam. Use this rule: for 24V, keep cable under 10m for 10A, under 5m for 20A. For 48V, you can double distance. Always use stranded copper cable for flexibility. Avoid aluminum â it corrodes in humid dam sites. Use cable lugs and crimp them properly. Test with multimeter after installation. Measure voltage at panel and at pump. Difference is drop. If over 3%, replace with thicker cable. Also consider temperature: in hot Africa, cable resistance increases. Derate by 10% for 40Â°C. So use next size up. Keep cables in conduit to avoid damage. Bury them 60cm deep if underground. Mark the route.

lessons.title: Grounding and Lightning Protection for Dam Sites
lessons.body: Lightning kills solar pumps in Africa. Dam sites are often open and wet, perfect for strikes. You need two things: equipment grounding and lightning protection. Equipment grounding connects metal parts (panel frames, pump body, controller box) to earth. This prevents shocks and fires. Use a copper-clad steel ground rod, 2m long, driven into moist soil near the dam. If soil is dry, use two rods 3m apart, bonded together. Connect with 6mmÂ² green/yellow copper wire. Run a separate ground wire from each panel frame to a common ground bus. Do not rely on conduit as ground. For lightning, install a lightning rod (air terminal) above the panels. It should be the highest point, at least 1m above panels. Use a 16mmÂ² copper wire from rod to ground rod. Keep the wire straight and avoid bends. Also install surge protection devices (SPDs) on DC side. A DC SPD costs about $50 and clamps voltage spikes. Put one at combiner box and one at controller. For AC side, use AC SPD. In Africa, many pumps fail after storms because of no SPD. Ground rods must be tested yearly with a ground resistance tester. Resistance should be under 10 ohms. If higher, add more rods or use bentonite clay to improve soil. Never ground to plastic pipes or building frames. Bond all grounds together. Use exothermic welding or proper clamps. Check connections after rain. Lightning season in West Africa is April to October. Inspect before then. A good ground system costs $200 but saves $2000 pump.

lessons.title: Junction Boxes, Combiner Boxes, and Disconnects
lessons.body: Junction boxes protect wire connections from water, dust, and sun. In Africa, use IP65 or IP68 rated boxes. IP65 means dust-tight and water-resistant. IP68 can be submerged. For dam sites, IP65 is minimum. Use PVC or polycarbonate boxes, not metal, because metal rusts. Combiner boxes combine multiple solar panel strings into one output. If you have 4 panels, each 12V, you might wire them in series-parallel. A combiner box has fuses for each string and a main disconnect. For a 24V system with 4 x 100W panels, you might have 2 strings of 2 panels in series. Each string gives 24V, 8A. Combiner box fuses: 10A per string. Main cable from combiner to controller must handle total current. Disconnects let you turn off power safely. Use a DC-rated disconnect switch, not an AC switch. DC switches have magnets to blow out arcs. Place disconnect between panels and controller, and between controller and pump. Label them clearly:

. In Africa, many installers skip disconnects, then get shocked during maintenance. Use lockable disconnects. Mount boxes on a pole or wall, 1.5m above ground. Face them away from afternoon sun. Use cable glands to seal entries. Silicone sealant around glands. Check boxes monthly for water. Drill a small drain hole at bottom if needed. Keep a wiring diagram inside the box. Use ferrules on wire ends for good contact. Tighten terminals to 2.5 Nm. Never leave exposed copper.

lessons.title: Electrical Safety Standards and Codes
lessons.body: In Africa, solar pump installations must follow national codes and international standards. The key ones are IEC 60364 for electrical installations, and IEC 62548 for PV arrays. Many countries have their own, like NRS 097 in South Africa, or KEBS in Kenya. Always check local rules. Basic safety: use double-insulated tools. Wear rubber gloves when working on DC. DC voltage above 50V is dangerous. A 48V system can kill. Never touch both terminals. Use one hand rule. Lock out/tag out before maintenance. Put a padlock on disconnect and keep key with you. Use correct cable colors: red for positive, black for negative, green/yellow for earth. In AC, brown live, blue neutral. Label all cables at both ends. Use conduit for all wiring. In Africa, UV degrades cable fast. Use UV-resistant cable or conduit. Keep cable off ground. Minimum burial depth 60cm. Use warning tape 30cm above buried cable. Install residual current device (RCD) on AC side if inverter used. RCD trips at 30mA. Test monthly. For DC, use fuses or breakers rated for DC. Never use AC breakers on DC. They may not extinguish arc. Use proper DC isolators. Grounding must be to earth, not neutral. In Africa, many pumps are stolen. Use tamper-proof screws on boxes. Keep documentation. After installation, test insulation resistance with a megohmmeter. Should be >1 MÎ©. Record all test results. Train users on safety. No children near pump. Post warning signs. First aid kit with rubber gloves and dry powder fire extinguisher for electrical fires.

lessons.title: Wiring Diagrams and Schematics
lessons.body: A wiring diagram shows how components connect. A schematic uses symbols. You need both. For a solar pump, start with a block diagram: panels -> combiner box -> controller -> pump. Add disconnect switches and fuses. Then draw detailed wiring. Use standard symbols: panel = rectangle with diagonal line, battery = long/short lines, pump = circle with M, controller = box with terminals. Draw DC positive in red, negative in black. Show wire sizes and colors. For a 24V system, draw two 12V panels in series. Positive of panel 1 to negative of panel 2. Then positive of panel 2 to combiner positive. Negative of panel 1 to combiner negative. From combiner, positive to fuse, then to controller PV+. Negative to controller PV-. Controller output to pump: positive to pump+, negative to pump-. Add ground symbol (three horizontal lines) to panel frames and pump body. For AC, draw inverter output: live to pump live, neutral to pump neutral, earth to pump earth. Include RCD. Use a CAD program like AutoCAD or free QElectroTech. Or draw by hand on graph paper. In Africa, many technicians use hand-drawn diagrams. That's fine if clear. Always keep a laminated copy in the controller box. Label each wire with number tags. Use wire markers. After installation, update diagram if you change anything. For troubleshooting, a diagram saves hours. Measure voltage at each point: panel, combiner, controller, pump. Compare to diagram. If voltage missing, trace back. Teach the pump owner to read the diagram. Show them how to turn off and on. Use colors in diagram. Red for positive, black for negative, green for earth. Blue for AC neutral. Brown for AC live. Keep it simple. One page per system.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Electrical System Design and Wiring for Solar Pumps on Dams

This practical reference consolidates the core design values, tables, and field rules that solar pump installers and agribusiness operators across Africa need when wiring a pump system fed from a dam or reservoir. It is written for commercial growers, irrigation service companies, and EPC contractors who must deliver systems that run for 10â20 years under high irradiance, dust, humidity, and lightning-prone conditions. Every figure here is drawn from published standards or manufacturer datasheets so that you can specify, quote, and commission with confidence.

The commercial logic is simple: a pump that fails because of undersized cable, a poor earth, or a missing surge arrester costs far more than the copper and hardware required to do it properly. Downtime during a dry spell can wipe out a season's margin. Treat the electrical bill of materials as an insurance policy, not an overhead.

DC and AC Wiring Basics

Solar pumping systems use DC on the array side and either DC or AC on the motor side. DC circuits are more sensitive to voltage drop because the same current flows through longer runs, and DC arcs do not self-extinguish at zero crossing. This means DC isolators must be rated for DC, not AC, and polarity must be observed on every connector. AC motors, by contrast, tolerate longer cable runs and are easier to protect with conventional breakers, but they need a correctly sized inverter or VFD and a clean earth reference.

For a dam site, the pump is usually 20â80 m from the controller and possibly hundreds of metres from the array. That distance drives cable sizing more than any other factor. Use flexible, UV-rated, tinned-copper cable for the array side, and submersible-rated cable (e.g. NSSHÃU or equivalent) for the drop into the dam. Never use standard building wire in a wet riser.

Cable Sizing and Voltage Drop

The design rule for solar pumping is to keep total voltage drop below 3% on the DC side and below 5% on the AC side. The formula for DC is:

Vdrop = (2 Ã L Ã I Ã Ï) / A

where L is one-way length in metres, I is current in amps, Ï is resistivity (0.0175 Î©Â·mmÂ²/m for copper at 20 Â°C), and A is cross-sectional area in mmÂ². The factor 2 accounts for the return conductor.

Table 1 gives practical cable sizes for the most common African solar pump configurations, assuming copper conductors and a maximum 3% drop on a 300 V DC array.

â  SAFETY WARNING â DC ARCS AND DAM SITE HAZARDS

PV arrays produce dangerous DC voltage whenever exposed to light, even when the controller is switched off. Never open a DC combiner box or disconnect a DC cable under load â DC arcs do not self-extinguish and can cause severe burns or fire. On dam sites, always isolate the array at the combiner, verify zero voltage with a CAT III rated meter, and lock off. Water and electricity together mean that any damaged cable insulation, flooded junction box, or missing gland must be treated as a live hazard. Use residual current devices (RCDs) rated 30 mA on AC circuits, and ensure all metalwork is bonded to a single earth electrode before energising.

Grounding and Lightning Protection

Dam sites are often the highest point in a field, making them prime lightning targets. A proper system needs three separate but bonded elements: equipment earthing (frame, controller, pump housing), lightning equipotential bonding, and surge protective devices (SPDs). Drive a copper-bonded earth rod at least 2.4 m deep near the controller, and bond the array frame, combiner enclosure, controller chassis, and pump head to it with 16 mmÂ² green/yellow copper. Measure resistance with a clamp meter; aim for under 10 Î©, and under 5 Î© in high-lightning regions such as the highveld of South Africa or the East African highlands.

Install Type 2 DC SPDs in the combiner box and Type 2 AC SPDs at the controller output. For long array runs, add a Type 1 SPD at the array end. In areas with more than 20 thunderstorm days per year, consider a lightning air terminal and down conductor separated from the electrical earth by at least 1 m.

Junction Boxes, Combiner Boxes, and Disconnects

Use IP65 or better enclosures for all outdoor boxes. Combiner boxes should include fused string protection, a DC isolator, and an SPD. Junction boxes in the riser must be gel-filled or potted if they will be submerged. Every disconnect must be lockable and labelled with the circuit reference and voltage. For dam sites, mount boxes above the high-water mark and provide a drip loop on all cables entering the enclosure.

Electrical Safety Standards and Codes

The primary international reference is IEC 60364, with Part 7-712 covering PV systems. In South Africa, SANS 10142-1 applies; in Kenya, the Energy Act and EPRA regulations; in Nigeria, NIS 1000 and SON standards. For solar pumping specifically, IEC 62253 covers photovoltaic pumping systems â design qualification and type approval. Always check the local utility and irrigation board requirements before commissioning.

Wiring Diagrams and Schematics

Every installation should have an as-built single-line diagram, a DC string layout, and a termination schedule. Keep a laminated copy in the controller enclosure. The single-line diagram above is a good template: it shows the array, combiner, controller, pump, and earth in one view, which is what a maintenance technician needs at 6 a.m. when the pump will not start.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Confirm array Vmp and Imp, then size DC cable for â¤3% voltage drop using Table 1.
  • Use only DC-rated isolators and fuses; never substitute AC components on the array side.
  • Bond array frame, combiner, controller, and pump to one earth electrode; measure resistance <10 Î©.
  • Install Type 2 DC SPD in combiner and Type 2 AC SPD at controller output.
  • Mount all enclosures above high-water mark, IP65 minimum, with drip loops and correct glands.
  • Label every disconnect with circuit reference, voltage, and lock-off point.
  • Verify polarity and insulation resistance before first energisation; record values in commissioning sheet.
  • Provide as-built single-line diagram and termination schedule inside the controller enclosure.

Further Reading

  • IEC 60364-7-712 â Low-voltage electrical installations: PV power supply systems (IEC)
  • IRENA â Solar Pumping for Irrigation: Improving Livelihoods and Sustainability (free PDF)
  • Grundfos SQFlex â Installation and Operating Instructions (free download)
  • US DOE Solar Energy Technologies Office â PV system design resources
  • SABS â SANS 10142-1: Wiring of premises (South African National Standards)

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of using DC instead of AC for a small solar pump?
options: A) DC is safer to touch
B) DC avoids inverter cost and losses
C) DC works better in rain
quiz.explanation: DC systems do not need an inverter, reducing cost and energy loss.

quiz.q: How do you wire two 12V panels to get 24V?
quiz.explanation: Series wiring adds voltage while current stays the same.

quiz.q: What color are MC4 connectors for positive and negative?
quiz.explanation: Standard MC4 connectors use red for positive and black for negative.

quiz.q: Why must you use a DC-rated switch on a DC circuit?
options: A) AC switches are more expensive
B) DC arcs are harder to break
D) AC switches have wrong color
quiz.explanation: DC arcs do not self-extinguish like AC arcs, so DC switches have special arc suppression.

quiz.q: For a 500W pump at 24V, what is the approximate current?
quiz.explanation: Current = Power / Voltage = 500W / 24V â 20.8A, rounded to 21A.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended voltage drop for a solar pump system?
quiz.explanation: Keeping voltage drop under 3% ensures the pump receives enough voltage to run efficiently.

quiz.q: Which cable size has the lowest resistance per meter?
quiz.explanation: Larger cross-sectional area means lower resistance; 10mmÂ² has the least resistance among the options.

quiz.q: If voltage drop is too high, what is the best solution?
options: B) Move panels closer to pump
quiz.explanation: Shortening the cable run reduces voltage drop more effectively than other changes.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid aluminum cable at a dam site?
options: B) It corrodes in humid conditions
D) It has higher resistance than copper
quiz.explanation: Aluminum corrodes quickly in damp environments, leading to poor connections.

quiz.q: What tool do you use to test voltage drop after installation?
quiz.explanation: A multimeter measures voltage at different points to calculate drop.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of equipment grounding?
options: B) To prevent shocks and fires
quiz.explanation: Grounding provides a safe path for fault current, preventing electric shock and fire.

quiz.q: What is the minimum length of a ground rod for a dam site?
quiz.explanation: A 2m copper-clad steel rod is standard for good earth contact.

quiz.q: Where should a lightning rod be placed?
options: B) At the same height as panels
quiz.explanation: The lightning rod must be the highest point to intercept strikes.

quiz.q: What device clamps voltage spikes on the DC side?
quiz.explanation: A surge protection device (SPD) limits transient overvoltages.

quiz.q: What is the maximum acceptable ground resistance?
quiz.explanation: Ground resistance should be under 10 ohms for effective protection.

quiz.q: What does IP65 rating mean?
quiz.explanation: IP65 means protection against dust and water jets.

quiz.q: Why should combiner box fuses be rated per string?
options: B) To protect each string from overcurrent
quiz.explanation: Individual string fuses prevent a fault in one string from affecting others.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a disconnect switch?
options: B) To safely turn off power for maintenance
C) To convert DC to AC
quiz.explanation: Disconnects allow isolation of circuits for safe servicing.

quiz.q: Where should junction boxes be mounted?
quiz.explanation: Mounting at 1.5m keeps boxes away from water and easy to access.

quiz.q: What is the correct torque for terminal screws in junction boxes?
quiz.explanation: 2.5 Nm is a standard torque for small electrical terminals.

quiz.q: Which standard covers PV array installations?
quiz.explanation: IEC 62548 specifically addresses photovoltaic array design and safety.

quiz.q: What is the one-hand rule in electrical safety?
options: A) Use only one hand when working on live circuits
B) Keep one hand in your pocket
C) Use one tool at a time
quiz.explanation: Using one hand reduces the risk of current passing through your heart.

quiz.q: What does an RCD trip at?
quiz.explanation: A 30mA RCD protects people from electric shock.

quiz.q: Why should you not use an AC breaker on a DC circuit?
options: B) It may not extinguish the arc
D) It has wrong voltage rating
quiz.explanation: AC breakers lack arc suppression needed for DC faults.

quiz.q: What is the minimum burial depth for underground cable?
quiz.explanation: 60cm depth protects cable from damage and temperature extremes.

quiz.q: What symbol represents a solar panel in a wiring diagram?
options: C) Long and short parallel lines
quiz.explanation: A rectangle with a diagonal line is the standard symbol for a PV panel.

quiz.q: What color is used for earth wire in a schematic?
quiz.explanation: Green/yellow is the universal color for earth/ground conductors.

quiz.q: Why keep a laminated wiring diagram in the controller box?
quiz.explanation: A diagram helps technicians trace faults quickly.

quiz.q: What should you do after changing any wiring?
quiz.explanation: Keeping the diagram current ensures future maintenance is accurate.

quiz.q: What is the first step in troubleshooting using a diagram?
options: B) Measure voltage at each point
quiz.explanation: Measuring voltage at key points helps locate where the circuit fails.
